title: The Ghost Ship: Mary Celeste
lines: December 1872. Sailors spot a ship drifting in the middle of the Atlantic. Her sails are up. Her cargo is untouched. There's food on board for six months. But there's not a single person on board.
Ten people had set sail on the Mary Celeste, including the captain's wife and their two-year-old daughter. None of them were ever seen again.
So what makes a captain abandon a perfectly good ship, in the middle of the ocean, with his own family? To find out, we go back one month.
November 1872. New York. Captain Benjamin Briggs, a careful and experienced sailor, sets out for Genoa, Italy. In the hold: 1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol.
The voyage is calm. On November 25th, the last entry in the ship's log notes an island in the Azores. Nothing unusual. Then, the log goes silent.
Nine days later, another ship, the Dei Gratia, finds her drifting between the Azores and Portugal. Her crew climbs aboard.
Below deck, everything is damp, but in order. The crew's boots and pipes are still there. Their belongings are untouched. But the only lifeboat is gone.
No sign of a storm. No sign of a fight. Nothing stolen. So why would ten people leave the safest place in the ocean, for a tiny open boat?
You might have heard the tea was still warm on the table. That's a myth. It comes from a story written by a young Arthur Conan Doyle, before he created Sherlock Holmes.
The real clues were stranger. The hatches were open. And when the cargo was unloaded in Italy, nine of the barrels were empty. That may be the key to everything.
One theory: fumes from those barrels built up below deck. If Briggs smelled them, or heard a rumble from the hold, he may have feared the ship was about to explode.
So he got everyone into the lifeboat, still tied to the ship by a long rope, and waited.
In 2006, a chemist recreated that scenario in a lab. The alcohol vapor exploded in a flash of flame, but left no scorch marks. Just like the empty ship.
And if that rope snapped, the Mary Celeste would have sailed on without them. Ten people, alone in a tiny boat, in the middle of the Atlantic.
As for the ship? Thirteen years later, her last captain ran her onto a reef in Haiti, on purpose, for the insurance money.
